# Getting started with R {#sec-getting-started-with-r}

This book is not an R tutorial. It is a book about Bayesian reasoning
that happens to use R to do the arithmetic, and you can get most of the
value from it without writing a line of code — see
[How to use the code in this book](#sec-r-how-to-use) below.

But several readers of the draft told me the same thing: they wanted to
follow along, and nothing in the book told them how to get to a point
where they could. This appendix fixes that. It is a signpost, not a
course — enough to get R running, plus pointers to the people who teach
it properly. 

## Installing R and an editor {#sec-r-install}

You need two things, and they are separate: **R** itself, which does the
computing, and an **editor**, which is where you actually work. Installing
only the first leaves you at a bare console; almost nobody works that way.

### Step 1 — install R

Download it from **<https://cran.r-project.org>**. This is CRAN, the
Comprehensive R Archive Network — the official home of R, run by the R
Foundation. Pick your operating system, take the latest release, accept
the defaults.

::: callout-tip
## Make sure you are on the real site

R and its editors are free, which unfortunately makes them attractive
bait for lookalike download sites. The two addresses worth trusting are
`cran.r-project.org` for R and `posit.co` for the editor. If you arrived
somewhere else via a search result, close the tab and type the address
in directly.

If you work somewhere with a managed software catalogue, check it first
— many organisations already offer R and RStudio there, sometimes as a
supported enterprise build, which saves you the download and the
conversation with IT.
:::

### Step 2 — install an editor

You have two good options, both free and both from Posit (the company
that employs many of the tidyverse developers).

-   **RStudio Desktop** — <https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/>.
    The standard choice, and the one nearly every tutorial you will find
    online assumes. Start here if you have no reason not to.
-   **Positron** — <https://positron.posit.co>. Posit's newer editor,
    built on the same foundations as VS Code. It handles R and Python
    equally well and has a built-in AI assistant. It is what I wrote this
    book in.

Either works for everything in this book. If you are undecided, take
RStudio: when you get stuck and search for help, the answer will be
written for RStudio.

### Step 3 — install the packages

Base R does relatively little on its own. Everything interesting comes
from **packages** — bundles of functions somebody else wrote and shared.
Run this **once**, in the console (the pane you type into directly), not
in a code chunk:

```r
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "peopleanalyticsdata", "skimr"))
```

That covers Chapters 1 to 3. The Bayesian modelling chapters need `brms`,
which is a larger install because it compiles models behind the scenes:

```r
install.packages("brms")
```

On some systems `brms` also needs a working C++ toolchain. If it
complains, the current instructions are maintained at
<https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanr/articles/cmdstanr.html> — follow those
rather than anything you find on a forum, because this is one of the few
areas where old advice goes stale quickly.

### If you would rather not install anything

**Posit Cloud** (<https://posit.cloud>) runs RStudio in a browser with a
free tier. Nothing to install, nothing to persuade IT to approve, and it
is a perfectly reasonable way to work through the Foundations chapters.
The free tier limits how many hours a month you get and how much memory
a project can use, which is fine for Chapters 1 to 3 and will start to
pinch once you are fitting Bayesian models.

## The packages this book leans on {#sec-r-packages}

Two names appear constantly and are worth knowing properly, because the
book treats them as background furniture.

### tidyverse

The **tidyverse** is not one package but a collection of them, designed
to work together and sharing a common style. When you run
`library(tidyverse)` you load about eight at once. The ones you will see
in this book:

| Package | What it does |
|---|---|
| `dplyr` | Manipulating tables — filter rows, add columns, group and summarise. Most of the code in this book is `dplyr`. |
| `ggplot2` | Every chart in this book. |
| `tibble` | A modern data frame — the table type most functions here return. |
| `tidyr` | Reshaping tables between long and wide. |
| `readr` | Reading data files in. |

The unifying idea is **tidy data**: one row per observation, one column
per variable, one value per cell. Chapter 1 introduces this properly. The
tidyverse is built around the assumption that your data is in that shape,
which is why its functions compose so neatly with one another.

### brms

**brms** — "Bayesian Regression Models using Stan" — is the package that
fits nearly every model from Chapter 6 onwards. It lets you write a
Bayesian model using the same formula syntax as R's ordinary regression
functions:

```r
brm(sales ~ performance + (1 | region), data = salespeople)
```

and then does the genuinely hard part — translating that into Stan,
compiling it, and sampling from the posterior — without you having to
write Stan yourself. It is the reason this book can teach Bayesian
modelling at all without a chapter of C++.

You do not need to understand any of that to read the book. Chapter 6
introduces `brms` where it is first needed, and Chapter 11 explains what
the sampling underneath is actually doing.

## How to use the code in this book {#sec-r-how-to-use}

Readers arrive here from very different places, so here is the honest
guidance.

-   **New to R, or new to statistics.** Run the code. Type it rather than
    pasting it, change a number, break it, see what the error says. The
    Foundations chapters are deliberately gentle for exactly this reason,
    and the fluency you build there is what makes the later chapters
    readable.
-   **Comfortable with statistics but not with R.** You can read past the
    code and still follow every argument in this book — the prose carries
    the reasoning and the output is always interpreted in words. What you
    should not skip is the Foundations part itself, because the Bayesian
    way of thinking about a probability is a genuine mental shift, and
    Chapters 2 and 3 are where that shift starts.
-   **Comfortable with both.** Skim Foundations for the framing, then
    start properly at Chapter 4.

::: callout-note
## On using an AI assistant to write the code

If you can describe your approach clearly in plain language, an AI
assistant can usually turn it into working R. That is a legitimate way
to work and I use it myself — but the description has to be *yours*.
Knowing what you want to compute is the analytical skill; producing the
syntax is not. @sec-llms sets out how to do this well, and
where it goes wrong.
:::

## Where to learn R properly {#sec-r-learning}

I am not going to teach R here when others do it better and keep it
current. These are the resources I actually point people to.

### The cheatsheets

Posit publishes one-page reference cards for each major package, and they
are the single most useful thing on this list — print the `dplyr` one and
keep it next to you.

**<https://posit.co/resources/cheatsheets/>**

The **Data transformation with dplyr** sheet is the one to start with. It
covers `filter()`, `select()`, `group_by()`, `summarise()` and
`mutate()` — including `mutate()`, which this book uses without ever
teaching formally. `mutate()` adds or changes a column; it is the verb
you reach for whenever an exercise asks you to derive something new from
what you already have, such as bucketing a numeric variable into groups.

### Books, free online

-   **R for Data Science** (Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel & Grolemund) —
    <https://r4ds.hadley.nz>. The standard introduction to the
    tidyverse, and the one to work through if you want to be able to
    write the code in this book yourself rather than read it.
-   **Handbook of Regression Modeling in People Analytics** (Keith
    McNulty) — <https://peopleanalytics-regression-book.org>. The
    frequentist companion to what this book does, on much of the same
    data, since the `peopleanalyticsdata` package is his.

### Built-in help

Inside R, `?function_name` opens the documentation for anything —
`?mutate`, `?rbinom`, `?set.seed`. The **Examples** section at the bottom
is usually the fastest way in; the rest of the page is written for
people who already know the answer.

@sec-further-reading has the wider reading list, including the
Bayesian texts this book draws on.
